Executive Summary Large power transformers (LPTs) are indispensable to U.S. hydropower operations, serving as generator step-up units that interconnect hydropower facilities to the high-voltage transmission grid. Their reliability is central to hydropower rehabilitation and grid modernization efforts, yet the LPT supply chain faces mounting stress from aging infrastructure, limited domestic production, and long lead times. This report is a supplement to the 2024 Hydropower Supply Chain Gap Analysis report (Putsche et al. 2024). It focuses specifically on the unique vulnerabilities of LPTs and their secondary components in the context of hydropower rehabilitation projects. The analysis herein includes insights gleaned from interviews with hydropower original equipment manufacturers, vendors, developers, and asset owners regarding their experiences with the LPT supply chain and its challenges. The Hydropower Supply Chain Gap Analysis investigated supply chain issues to expand domestic manufacturing for hydropower technologies emphasizing the need for a strong supply chain to ensure future clean energy and grid reliability needs. Several key issues were identified in the Hydropower Supply Chain Gap Analysis report, such as hydropower component demand, which is irregular and difficult to forecast primarily because of long asset lifetimes and limiting incentives for domestic investment. In addition, there is a notable lack of domestic manufacturing for key components such as large turbines, hydrogenerators, and electrical steel. In fact, some components have no domestic source. Other issues include federal procurement practices based on up-front cost, strong foreign competition, and the availability of skilled labor. These issues clearly indicate that without further efforts to improve demand signals and supply chain conditions, the U.S. hydropower supply chain will be limited in its ability to meet future energy needs. The U.S. hydropower fleet is among the oldest in the world, with an average plant age of nearly 80 years. Many units now require modernization, including the replacement or refurbishment of LPTs. However, procurement timelines for new transformers measured from purchase order to receipt have lengthened from 12–18 months to 30–36 months (U.S. Government Accountability Office 2023) for typical LPTs. For the extra-high-voltage transformer units, lead time can extend up to 60 months (U.S. Department of Energy 2024) due to complex engineering requirements, which creates significant risks for project scheduling and grid reliability. Costs have also risen sharply, with LPT prices in 2025 roughly 50% to 70% higher than their 2019 baseline (Wood Mackenzie 2025). A primary bottleneck is upstream material supply. Grain-oriented electrical steel, which forms the magnetic core of transformers, is produced domestically, but U.S. output is constrained in both grade variety and total volume relative to demand.
